passages.source_text: λέγουσι γὰρ οἱ πολλοὶ Τῶν σεβασμάτων ἡμῶν σέβομεν οὐ τὸν χρυσὸν οὐδὲ τὸν ἄργυρον οὐδὲ ξύλον ἢ λίθον (ἴσμεν γὰρ καὶ ἡμεῖς ὅτι ταῦτα οὐδέν ἐστιν ἢ ἄψυχος ὕλη καὶ ἀνθρώπου θνητοῦ τέχνη), ἀλλὰ τὸ κατοικοῦν ἐν αὐτοῖς πνεῦμα, τοῦτο θεὸν λέγομεν. ὁρᾶτ’ οὖν τῶν ταῦτα λεγόντων τὴν κακοήθειαν. ἐπεὶ γὰρ τὸ φαινόμενον εὐέλεγκτόν ἐστιν ὅτι οὐδέν ἐστιν, κατέφυγον ἐπὶ τὸ ἀόρατον, ὡς ἐπ’ ἀδήλῳ τινὶ ἐλεγχθῆναι μὴ δυνάμενοι. πλὴν συνομολογοῦσιν ἡμῖν οἱ τοιοῦτοι ἐπὶ μέρους ὅτι τὸ ἥμισυ τῶν παρ’ αὐτοῖς ἱδρυμάτων· θεὸς οὐκ ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ ἀναίσθητος ὕλη. λοιπὸν δὲ περιλείπεται δεῖξαι αὐτοῖς πῶς πιστεύομεν ὅτι· θεῖον ἔχει πνεῦμα. ἀλλ’ ἐπιδεῖξαι ἡμῖν οὐ δύναται ὅτι ἔστιν, ἐπεὶ μὴ ἔστιν — καὶ αὐτοῖς ἑωρακέναι οὐ πιστεύομεν. ἡμεῖς αὐτοῖς ὅτι θεῖον οὐκ ἔχει πνεῦμα τὰς ἀποδείξεις παρέξομεν, ὅπως τοῦ δοκεῖν αὐτὰ ἔνπνοα εἶναι οἱ φιλαλήθεις τὸν ἔλεγχον ἀκούσαντες τῆς λυσσώδους ὑπονοίας ἀποτράπωνται.

τὸ μὲν δὴ πρῶτον, εἰ ὡς ἔμπνοα ὄντα σέβεσθε αὐτά, τί καὶ ἀνθρώπων; ἀρχαίων τάφους προσκυνεῖτε, τῶν ὁμολογουμένως οὐδὲ πνεῦμα θεῖον ἐσχηκότων; οὕτως οὐδὲ κατὰ τοῦτο ἀληθεύετε. πλὴν εἰ ὄντως ἔνπνοα ἦν τὰ σεβάσματα ὑμῶν, ἀφ’ ἑαυτῶν ἂν ἐκινεῖτο, φωνὴν ἂν εἶχεν, τὴν ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς ἀράχνην ἀπεσείετο, τοὺς αὐτοῖς ἐπιβουλεῦσαι θέλοντας καὶ κλέπτοντας ἀπεωθεῖτο ἄν, τοὺς τὰ ἀναθήματα ἀποσυλῶντας συνελάμβανεν ἂν ῥᾳδίως. νῦν δὲ τούτων οὐδὲν ποιοῦσιν, ἀλλ’ ὡς κατάδικοι (καὶ μάλιστα οἱ τιμιώτεροι αὐτῶν) φρουροῦνται, ὡς καὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν εἰρήκαμεν. τί δέ; οὐ φόρους καὶ τέλη ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἀπαιτοῦσιν ὑμᾶς οἱ δυνάσται ὡς πολλὰ καρπιζομένους τῶν ἐκεῖ;. τί δέ; οὐ πολλάκις ὑπὸ πολεμίων διηρπάγησαν καὶ συντριβέντες διενεμήθησαν; οὐχὶ καὶ τῶν ἔξω θρησκευόντων αὐτοὶ πλέον οἱ ἱερεῖς, ἐπὶ τῇ ἀχρήστῳ θρησκείᾳ ἑαυτῶν κατεγνωκότες, τῶν ἀναθημάτων πολλὰ ὑφαιροῦνται;

ναί φησιν, ἀλλὰ προνοίᾳ αὐτῶν ἐφωράθησαν. ψεῦδός ἐστιν. πόσοι γὰρ οὐκ ἐφωράθησαν αὐτῶν; εἰ δὲ διὰ τὸ ἐνίους συνειλῆφθαι δύναμιν αὐτοὺς ἔχειν λέγουσιν, πεπλάνηνται. καὶ γὰρ τῶν τυμβωρύχων τινὲς μὲν εὑρίσκονται, τινὲς δὲ λανθάνουσιν, καὶ οὐ δήπου γε τῇ τῶν νεκρῶν δυνάμει οἱ συλληφθέντες ἐφωράθησαν. τοιοῦτόν τι καὶ περὶ τοὺς κλεπτομένους καὶ συλωμένους θεοὺς ἔστιν ἡμῖν νοεῖν. ἀλλὰ (φησίν) οὐ πεφροντίκασιν τῶν ξοάνων αὐτῶν οἱ ἐν αὐτοῖς ὄντες θεοί. τί οὖν αὐτὰ ὑμεῖς τημελεῖτε σμήχοντες καὶ πλύνοντες καὶ καθαίροντες, στεφανοῦντες, ἐπιθύοντες; διόπερ ἐντεῦθεν συννοήσατε μηδὲ ὀρθῷ λογισμῷ ποιοῦντες. ὡς γὰρ τοῖς νεκροῖς ἐπικλαίετε, οὕτω καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς ὑμῶν ἐπιθύετε καὶ σπένδετε.

οὐκέτι μέντοι τοῦτο οὐδὲ τῷ τοῦ Καίσαρος καὶ τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτὸν ἐξουσιῶν συμφωνεῖ παραδείγματι, διοικητὰς αὐτοὺς λέγειν, ὁπότε ὑμεῖς αὐτῶν τὴν πᾶσαν ποιεῖσθε πρόνοιαν, ὡς προεῖπον, κατὰ πάντα τημελοῦντες ὑμῶν τὰ ἱδρύματα. αὐτὰ γὰρ οὐδὲν δυνάμενα οὐδὲν ποιεῖ. ἐπεὶ εἴπατε ἡμῖν τί διοικοῦσιν; τί ποιοῦσιν τοιοῦτον ὁποῖόν τι οἱ κατὰ τόπον ἡγούμενοι; τί δὲ ἐνεργοῦσιν τοιοῦτον ὁποῖον οἱ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀστέρες; εἰ μήτι φαίνουσιν ὡς ὁ ἥλιος, οἷς λύχνους ὑμεῖς ἅπτετε; μὴ ὥσπερ τὰ νέφη ὑετοὺς φέρει, καὶ αὐτοὶ φέρειν ὄμβρους δύνανται, οἱ μηδὲ ἑαυτοὺς κινεῖν δυνάμενοι, ἐὰν μὴ ἄνθρωποι ἐπιλάβωνται; ἢ καρποὺς παρέχονται τὸν αὐτὸν τῇ γῇ τρόπον οἷς ὑμεῖς θυσίας χορηγεῖτε; οὕτως οὐδὲν δύναται.

εἰ δὲ καὶ ποιεῖν τι ἐδύναντο, οὐκ ἂν αὐτοὺς ὀρθῶς θεοὺς ἐλέγετε, ὁπότε οὐδὲ τὰ στοιχεῖα ὀνομάζειν ἔξεστιν θεούς, δι’ ὧν τὰ ἀγαθὰ χορηγεῖται. ἀλλὰ τὸν μόνον τάξαντα αὐτὰ πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν χρῆσιν ἐκτελεῖν τὰ πάντα καὶ κελεύσαντα ἀνθρώπῳ ὑπηρετεῖν, μόνον ὀρθῷ λόγῳ θεὸν ὀνομάζομεν. οὗ τῆς εὐεργεσίας ὑμεῖς μὴ αἰσθανόμενοι τὰ ὑμῖν δοῦλα ἀπονεμηθέντα στοιχεῖα καθ’ αὐτῶν δεσπόζειν ἀνηγορεύσατε. καὶ τί περὶ στοιχείων δεῖ λέγειν; ὁπότε καὶ ἄψυχα ἀγάλματα πεποιηκότες οὐ μόνον προσκυνεῖτε, ἀλλ’ ὡς δοῦλοι κατὰ πάντα αὐτοῖς ὑποτετάχθαι ἀξιοῦτε. διὰ τοῦτο ἑαυτοὺς δι’ ὧν παρεφρονήσατε, δαίμοσιν ὑποχείριοι γεγόνατε. πλὴν διὰ τῆς εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν θεὸν ἐπιγνώσεως ἐκ τῶν καλῶν πράξεων δύνασθε δεσπόται γενέσθαι πάλιν καὶ δαίμοσιν ὡς δούλοις ἐπιτάξαι καὶ ὡς υἱοὶ θεοῦ αἰωνίου βασιλείας κληρονόμοι καταστῆναι.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: For most people say, “In our objects of worship, we venerate not the gold, nor the silver, nor wood or stone (for we too know that these are nothing other than lifeless matter and the craftsmanship of a mortal human), but the spirit dwelling in them; this is what we call a god.” See, then, the dishonesty of those who say this. For since what is visible is easily exposed as nothing, they have fled for refuge to the invisible, as though they could not be refuted about something uncertain. Nevertheless, such people agree with us in part that one half of the cult images among them is not a god but unfeeling matter. It remains for them to show how we are to believe that it has a divine spirit. Yet such a person cannot demonstrate to us that it exists, since it does not—and we do not believe that they have seen it themselves. We will provide them with proofs that it does not have a divine spirit, so that lovers of truth, on hearing the refutation of this rabid supposition, may turn away from thinking that these things are animate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: In our objects of worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: σεβάσματα denotes things treated as sacred or worthy of veneration; “objects of worship” preserves the cultic sense without assuming that they are divine.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἥμισυ τῶν παρ’ αὐτοῖς ἱδρυμάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: one half of the cult images among them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱδρύματα refers here to erected cult objects. “One half” preserves the argument that their alleged material-and-spirit composite is already conceded to be partly mere matter.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λοιπὸν δὲ περιλείπεται δεῖξαι αὐτοῖς πῶς πιστεύομεν ὅτι· θεῖον ἔχει πνεῦμα.
lexical_decisions.chosen: It remains for them to show how we are to believe that it has a divine spirit.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering construes αὐτοῖς with περιλείπεται and the infinitive as identifying those responsible for demonstrating the claim. Alternatively, αὐτοῖς may be the recipient of δεῖξαι: “it remains to show them how we believe that it has a divine spirit.” The main reading better anticipates the demand that follows for an opponent to demonstrate the spirit’s existence. πῶς πιστεύομεν could also be rendered indicatively as “how we believe,” but “how we are to believe” gives it deliberative or challenging force consistent with the speaker’s stated disbelief.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλ’ ἐπιδεῖξαι ἡμῖν οὐ δύναται ὅτι ἔστιν, ἐπεὶ μὴ ἔστιν — καὶ αὐτοῖς ἑωρακέναι οὐ πιστεύομεν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet such a person cannot demonstrate to us that it exists, since it does not—and we do not believe that they have seen it themselves.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular δύναται is taken as referring to a representative opponent, while the following αὐτοῖς resumes the opposing group in the plural. Because the subject of δύναται is unstated, an image or the alleged spirit could instead be understood as the subject: “Yet it cannot demonstrate to us that it exists.” The confirmed singular has not been regularized as a plural.

lexical_decisions.chosen: this rabid supposition
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόνοια can mean suspicion, notion, or supposition; here it is the hostile characterization of the belief that the images are animate. λυσσώδης supplies the forceful image of rabid madness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: animate
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective means possessing breath or life, in contrast with the objects’ lifeless material.

passages.text: First, then, if you venerate them as animate, why do you also bow down before the tombs of ancient people, who admittedly did not even possess a divine spirit? Thus you are not telling the truth in this respect either. Yet if your objects of worship really were animate, they would move by themselves, would have a voice, would shake off the cobweb on them, would repel those who wish to plot against them and who steal from them, and would easily seize those stripping away the votive offerings. But now they do none of these things. Instead, like condemned prisoners—and especially the more valuable among them—they are kept under guard, as we said at the outset. Again, do not the rulers demand taxes and duties from you on their account, on the ground that you derive great profit from the things there? And have they not often been plundered by enemies and, after being smashed, divided up? And do not the priests themselves, even more than those who worship from outside, having passed judgment against themselves over their useless worship, secretly remove many of the votive offerings?

lexical_decisions.chosen: the tombs of ancient people
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχαίων agrees with ἀνθρώπων in the genitive plural; together they identify whose tombs are meant. The English reads the wording continuously across the selected edition’s question mark, as disclosed in the punctuation note.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς αὐτοῖς ἐπιβουλεῦσαι θέλοντας καὶ κλέπτοντας
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who wish to plot against them and who steal from them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first participle expresses hostile intent and the second actual theft. The object of κλέπτοντας is unstated; “from them” fits the surrounding discussion of images and their offerings, while “who steal them” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the more valuable among them
lexical_decisions.rationale: τίμιος can mean honored or costly. The need to guard the objects from theft makes material value the more immediate sense, though “the more honored” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the ground that you derive great profit from the things there
lexical_decisions.rationale: καρπίζομαι denotes enjoying or reaping proceeds. τῶν ἐκεῖ is elliptical, referring to the things or resources located at the cult sites.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who worship from outside
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase distinguishes the priests from worshipers outside the priestly group; “lay worshipers” is a contextual alternative but is more interpretive.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῇ ἀχρήστῳ θρησκείᾳ ἑαυτῶν κατεγνωκότες
lexical_decisions.chosen: having passed judgment against themselves over their useless worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect participle presents the priests as having reached, or as standing in, an adverse judgment against themselves concerning their worship before or while they secretly remove the offerings. It does not state that the theft itself produces that judgment.

source_issues.source_quote: τί καὶ ἀνθρώπων; ἀρχαίων τάφους προσκυνεῖτε
source_issues.issue: The selected edition’s question mark separates ἀνθρώπων from the agreeing genitive adjective ἀρχαίων, although the surviving words form the coherent phrase “tombs of ancient people” when read continuously. This is treated provisionally as an editorial-punctuation irregularity, not as missing wording.
source_issues.proposed_reading: τί καὶ ἀνθρώπων ἀρχαίων τάφους προσκυνεῖτε;

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints both a Greek question mark and a period at the end of the question. The duplicated punctuation does not affect the recoverable syntax or wording.

passages.text: “Yes,” he says, “but they were detected through the gods’ providence.” This is false. For how many of them have gone undetected? If, because some have been caught, they say that those gods possess power, they are mistaken. Some tomb robbers too are discovered, while others escape notice, and surely those who are caught were not detected by the power of the dead. We can understand something similar about the gods that are stolen and despoiled. “But,” he says, “the gods within them have no concern for their own carved images.” Why, then, do you yourselves tend them—scrubbing, washing, and cleaning them, crowning them, and offering sacrifices to them? Therefore recognize from this that you are not acting with sound reasoning either. For just as you weep over the dead, so you also offer sacrifices and pour libations to your gods.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ναί φησιν, ἀλλὰ προνοίᾳ αὐτῶν ἐφωράθησαν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: “Yes,” he says, “but they were detected through the gods’ providence.”
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first plural referent is the thieves, while αὐτῶν refers contextually to the gods or cult images credited with providential action. The nouns are made explicit in English to prevent the two pronouns from being confused.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that those gods possess power
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative αὐτούς resumes the gods credited with detecting thieves, not the thieves who were caught.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοιοῦτόν τι καὶ περὶ τοὺς κλεπτομένους καὶ συλωμένους θεοὺς ἔστιν ἡμῖν νοεῖν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: We can understand something similar about the gods that are stolen and despoiled.
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔστιν with the dative and infinitive expresses the possibility or availability of understanding the analogous situation, rather than an obligation or recommendation. Both passive participles modify the gods themselves.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their own carved images
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξόανον originally denotes a carved, especially wooden, cult image and can more broadly denote an idol or statue. “Carved images” preserves that material sense without requiring that every object be wooden.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τημελεῖτε σμήχοντες καὶ πλύνοντες καὶ καθαίροντες, στεφανοῦντες, ἐπιθύοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: tend them—scrubbing, washing, and cleaning them, crowning them, and offering sacrifices to them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The sequence lists the physical and ritual care supplied by the worshipers. ἐπιθύω here means to offer sacrifice, not merely to desire.

passages.text: Yet calling them administrators no longer accords even with the analogy of Caesar and the authorities under him, when you yourselves take all care of them, as I said before, tending your cult images in every respect. For, capable of nothing, they do nothing. So tell us: what do they administer? What do they do comparable to what the rulers in each locality do? What do they accomplish comparable to God’s stars? Unless perhaps they shine like the sun—the very ones for whom you yourselves light lamps? Can they, just as the clouds bring rains, also bring downpours—they who cannot even move themselves unless people take hold of them? Or do they provide fruits in the same way as the earth—they for whom you supply sacrifices? Thus they can do nothing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: calling them administrators
lexical_decisions.rationale: διοικητής denotes one who manages, governs, or administers. “Administrators” maintains the comparison with Caesar’s subordinate authorities.

lexical_decisions.chosen: cult images
lexical_decisions.rationale: The erected objects are the material images being tended, illuminated, and physically moved; “cult images” conveys this setting better than the broader “institutions” or “establishments.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the rulers in each locality
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes leaders or governors assigned to particular places, continuing the administrative analogy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μήτι φαίνουσιν ὡς ὁ ἥλιος, οἷς λύχνους ὑμεῖς ἅπτετε;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Unless perhaps they shine like the sun—the very ones for whom you yourselves light lamps?
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰ μήτι introduces an ironic possible exception. The emphatic ὑμεῖς sharpens the contrast between supposedly shining gods and worshipers who must provide their light.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unless people take hold of them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle verb means to grasp or take hold of something; here people must handle the immobile images before they can move.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the same way as the earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative τῇ γῇ marks the earth as the standard of comparison for providing fruit.

passages.text: And even if they were able to do something, you would not rightly call them gods, since even the elements, through which good things are supplied, may not be called gods. But only the one who ordered them to carry out everything for our use and commanded them to serve humankind—him alone do we rightly call God. Unaware of his beneficence, you proclaimed that the elements assigned to you as servants were to rule over human beings. And why is there any need to speak about the elements, when you even make lifeless statues and not only bow down before them but also think it proper to be subjected to them in every respect as servants? For this reason, you yourselves, through the things by which you lost your senses, have become subject to demons. Nevertheless, through recognition of God himself, you can by good deeds become masters again, give orders to demons as servants, and, as sons of God, be established as heirs of an eternal kingdom.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the elements
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes the constituent powers or elements of the natural order through which benefits are supplied; the argument denies that their usefulness makes them gods.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν μόνον τάξαντα αὐτὰ πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν χρῆσιν ἐκτελεῖν τὰ πάντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: only the one who ordered them to carry out everything for our use
lexical_decisions.rationale: τάσσω expresses appointing or ordering the elements to perform their assigned functions for human use.

lexical_decisions.chosen: commanded them to serve humankind
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular ἀνθρώπῳ is generic, referring to humanity rather than one particular man.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ὑμῖν δοῦλα ἀπονεμηθέντα στοιχεῖα καθ’ αὐτῶν δεσπόζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: that the elements assigned to you as servants were to rule over human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes αὐτῶν as a notional plural resumption of the preceding generic ἀνθρώπῳ, “humankind.” Taking it as referring to the elements themselves or to the good things would produce a much less coherent claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς δοῦλοι κατὰ πάντα αὐτοῖς ὑποτετάχθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: to be subjected to them in every respect as servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: δοῦλοι marks complete subordinate status. “Servants” follows the supplied wording policy, while “slaves” would more explicitly foreground ownership and coercive subjection.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τοῦτο ἑαυτοὺς δι’ ὧν παρεφρονήσατε, δαίμοσιν ὑποχείριοι γεγόνατε
lexical_decisions.chosen: For this reason, you yourselves, through the things by which you lost your senses, have become subject to demons.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative ἑαυτούς is treated as a pendent emphatic expression resumed by the second-person verb. δι’ ὧν refers to the cult objects as the means or occasion of their loss of reason.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τῆς εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν θεὸν ἐπιγνώσεως ἐκ τῶν καλῶν πράξεων
lexical_decisions.chosen: through recognition of God himself, you can by good deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering attaches ἐκ τῶν καλῶν πράξεων to becoming masters again, while διὰ τῆς ... ἐπιγνώσεως gives the broader means. It could alternatively describe recognition of God as arising from good deeds.

lexical_decisions.chosen: give orders to demons as servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative phrase identifies the demons as the servants being commanded, reversing the preceding subjection to them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς υἱοὶ θεοῦ αἰωνίου βασιλείας κληρονόμοι καταστῆναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: as sons of God, be established as heirs of an eternal kingdom
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering attaches αἰωνίου to βασιλείας. Grammatically it could instead modify θεοῦ, yielding “as sons of the eternal God, be established as heirs of a kingdom,” but the chosen attachment gives the more natural division of the two genitive phrases.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ ὑμῖν δοῦλα ἀπονεμηθέντα στοιχεῖα καθ’ αὐτῶν δεσπόζειν ἀνηγορεύσατε
source_issues.issue: The plural αὐτῶν has no nearby plural human antecedent; its nearest explicit plural antecedents are the elements or the good things, neither of which gives the expected contrast. The translation defensibly treats it as a notional resumption of generic ἀνθρώπῳ, but καθ’ ὑμῶν, “over you,” is a plausible conjecture and is not the supplied reading.
source_issues.proposed_reading: τὰ ὑμῖν δοῦλα ἀπονεμηθέντα στοιχεῖα καθ’ ὑμῶν δεσπόζειν ἀνηγορεύσατε

source_issues.source_quote: διὰ τοῦτο ἑαυτοὺς δι’ ὧν παρεφρονήσατε, δαίμοσιν ὑποχείριοι γεγόνατε.
source_issues.issue: The accusative ἑαυτούς does not formally agree with the nominative predicate ὑποχείριοι and the second-person subject of γεγόνατε. It can be read as a pendent accusative emphasizing the people addressed, which supports the main rendering; nominative αὐτοί would be a possible conjectural regularization.
source_issues.proposed_reading: διὰ τοῦτο αὐτοὶ δι’ ὧν παρεφρονήσατε, δαίμοσιν ὑποχείριοι γεγόνατε.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
